The nadaswaram is a double-reed aerophone from Tamil Nadu, Hornbostel–Sachs 422.112.2. The body is conical, with a wooden or metal bell at the lower end, and it usually has seven fingerholes and five tuning holes that can be sealed with wax; it sounds with a double reed, and semitones and quarter tones are produced by adjusting the pressure and force of the airstream. It is often played in pairs, accompanied by the thavil drum, and an ottu oboe can supply a continuous note. In South Indian culture it is regarded as an auspicious instrument, a member of the family of auspicious instruments (mangala vadyam), and it is common at Hindu weddings, in temples and at South Indian traditional music events, and is also found in northern and eastern Sri Lanka.
印度納達斯瓦拉姆管為氣鳴雙簧樂器，傳統管身取用阿恰樹木，現亦見竹、檀香木、銅、黃: The nadaswaram is a double-reed aerophone; its body is traditionally made of achu wood, and bamboo, sandalwood, copper, brass, ebony and ivory are also used now; for wooden instruments old timber is preferred, sometimes wood taken from old houses. The reed is made of dried grass, a metal socket and a small metal tube at the top carry the mouthpiece, and the bell at the lower end is of wood or metal. An ivory or horn needle is supplied for cleaning the reed, and the five holes at the bottom of the tube can be sealed with wax to adjust the timbre.

納達斯瓦拉姆源自泰米爾納德邦，屬雙簧氣鳴樂器。約五世紀《西拉巴提伽拉姆》提及 v: The nadaswaram comes from Tamil Nadu and is a double-reed aerophone. The Silappatikaram, of about the fifth century, mentions a vangiyam whose construction matches the modern instrument; inscriptions of the mid-fifteenth century and the 1530s give nagaswaram or nakaswaram; the seventeenth-century Padasangraham also mentions the nagaswaram. It has since been used in southern India and in northern and eastern Sri Lanka, and has spread with Tamil emigrants. The modern instrument has seven holes, a double reed, a conical body and a bell, and is often played in pairs with thavil accompaniment.
納達斯瓦拉姆管為雙簧氣鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs編號422.112: The nadaswaram is a double-reed aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 422.112.2. Its conical body widens towards the lower end, which has a large bell; the sound is strong and powerful, among the loudest of the acoustic instruments that are not of brass. The range is about two and a half octaves and the fingering is close to that of the Indian bansuri; semitones and quarter tones are produced by adjusting the pressure and force of the blown airstream. There are five further holes lower on the body, which can be closed with wax to change the timbre. Compared with the North Indian shehnai it is longer and uses a double reed rather than a quadruple reed.
納達斯瓦拉姆管用於南印度泰米爾納德、安得拉邦、特蘭伽納、卡納塔克、喀拉拉及斯里蘭: The nadaswaram is used at Hindu weddings and temple rituals in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka and Kerala in southern India and in northern and eastern Sri Lanka; it is an auspicious instrument, mostly played out of doors. It is usually played in pairs, accompanied by a pair of thavil drums, and an ottu drone resembling an oboe can be added. The source also mentions its playing role in Tamil cinema, and that jazz musicians have played and recorded it.
